description: Tall steel mast carrying a cluster of four floodlight heads on a crossbar, for a court or temple fairground

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Very tall steel mast of round section, tapering as it rises from a wide square bolted base flange with a bolt-down shroud around its foot and a flat rectangular access door plate low on the shaft, and at the very top a horizontal crossbar carrying four floodlight heads in a row, each head a squat closed box tapering slightly toward a large flat rectangular lens on its front, all four hung below the crossbar on short yokes and tilted down together to the same angle Materials: Hot-dip galvanised steel gone dull matt grey with white zinc bloom, running rust streaks below the access door and around the base bolts, dirt and splash darkening the lowest metre, grey painted floodlight bodies chalky on the sunward side, grimy lenses with insect debris along their upper frames.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless pure WHITE studio matte. The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless white backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient. This is a studio cut-out, NOT an outdoor photograph: there must be no sky, no clouds, no buildings, no road and no overhead cables anywhere in the frame.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo. The lamp is switched OFF and emits no light.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 2.16 x 11.95 x 0.88 m. Cost: 540 triangles / 16000, 4 draw calls / 12, 2 materials / 8, 4 unique geometries / 16, 1 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.75, 1.0, 0.75], interior hole fractions [0.0614, 0.0, 0.0387, 0.0]).  The turntable gate runs with --allow-holes and the openings were PROVEN rather than assumed: the flagged rows read exactly 58,58,58 at alpha 0 -- the backdrop itself, seen between each yoke's two arms, which is what a yoke-hung floodlight is.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 2.160 x 11.950 x 0.880 m against the declared 2.2 x 12 x 1.0 -- within 2% on width and height, 12% under on depth. Depth runs from the baseplate's rear edge to the raked heads' glazed faces; the heads were pushed forward from an initial 0.786 m to close most of that gap, and the remaining 12% is the honest cost of not raking them further than the plate does.

Four heads from ONE INSTANCED GEOMETRY at four placements along the bar -- one draw call for all four, which the asset notes require explicitly. Each is a two-box trapezoid deeper at the back than at its glazed face, raked 35 degrees nose-down on a U yoke straddling the bar, with a cast rear boss. The previous build had bare quads with no housing, yoke or glass.

A tapered SQUARE mast 0.300 m at the foot to 0.185 m at the head, per the asset notes' 0.3 m shaft, with four triangular gussets welded up its faces from the baseplate and a chamfered cap. The previous build was a round pipe with none of it. Building the shaft as one frustum makes it 12 triangles, which is why four instanced heads and a crossbar still leave the prop at 3% of its ceiling.

Two material layers: galvanised steel for mast, gussets, plate and bar, and one instanced flood-housing material carrying housing, yoke and glass as vertex colours -- three tones on one material because splitting them would cost three draw calls per head instead of one for all four. Galvanised luma 158 is clear of the 55.5-60.5 window gatecrop erases. An earlier lift of the housing tone to luma 200 was made on a WRONG diagnosis of the gate's hole verdict and has been reverted; it moved the hole fraction by 0.0011.

A 0.56 m square plate with four proud 62 mm bolts, larger than the street columns' because this mast is 12 m and carries four heads, plus the four welded gussets that are what reads as a structural mast rather than a pipe pushed into a plate. The previous build had no baseplate at all.

name: Futsal Floodlight Mast
nameTh: เสาไฟส่องสว่างสนามกีฬา
notes:
The mast over a neighbourhood futsal court, a school field or a temple fairground -- shorter and cruder than a stadium mast, with the heads hung on a single crossbar rather than a ring. Sized from a 12 m mounting height; the crossbar is about 2 m across and the shaft about 0.3 m at the base. The four heads must be one instanced assembly repeated along the crossbar, which is the whole reason the prop stays cheap. budgetClass pinned to hero against the hero2x its 12 m height would derive, because a mast is one tapered cylinder plus that instanced head, and a court needs four of these standing in a level at once. Static: bolted to a foundation, so physics stays disabled.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED hero -> hero2x (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.
